title: FRIEDA: Cartographic Reasoning Benchmark
one_liner: A benchmark that tests whether vision-language models can read maps the way people do: by understanding symbols, measuring distances, and reasoning across multiple maps.
lead: Maps are nothing like charts. They use special symbols (squiggly lines for rivers, colored regions for countries, tiny numbers for elevations), compass arrows for orientation, and numbers for scale to encode meaning. When you read a map, you have to connect all these pieces: Which river is on the north side? How far apart are these two towns? What area did the earthquake shake? This is called cartographic reasoning, and it matters for disaster response and urban planning. But current vision-language models (the kind that look at images and answer questions) have barely been tested on it. FRIEDA is a benchmark—a test set with real maps from geology reports, urban planning documents, and environmental assessments—that exposes this gap.

problem.h2: Maps look like charts, but they are not
paras: When you read a chart, you look for bars or dots and read off a value. When you read a map, you have to decode a visual language: colored regions mean different things in different maps, symbols stand for physical features (a river, a road, a building), arrows point north, and numbers at the bottom tell you the scale (how many miles per inch). A chart is a direct picture of a data table. A map is a translation—it squashes the three-dimensional Earth onto a flat page and uses symbols to say what each piece means.

So far, vision-language models have been tested mostly on charts and infographics—simpler tasks where you just read the numbers directly. Some researchers tried testing them on maps, but only simple ones, one at a time, or focused on specific domains like satellite imagery. This left a huge gap: Can a model read real maps the way a person does—understanding the layer of symbolic meaning, comparing multiple maps from the same document, and reasoning across them to answer multi-step questions?

callout.html: FRIEDA is a benchmark with real maps from actual documents, designed to test whether vision-language models can truly read and reason about maps.

steps.text: Source actual maps from geology, urban planning, environmental documents.
Tag each map for topological (inside, border, touching), metric (distance), and directional (north, south) questions.
Write multi-step questions, some single-map, some requiring cross-map reasoning and retrieval.
Run 11 leading vision-language models in two modes: direct (map given) and contextual (find the map first).
Compare model accuracy to human performance and categorize errors by reasoning type.

paras: FRIEDA is a benchmark dataset: a collection of real maps paired with carefully designed questions that force models to do authentic cartographic reasoning. The object is not a model or an algorithm. It is a set of test cases that expose whether models actually understand maps.

hidden.name: model-to-human performance drop
paras: This is the chasm between what a trained vision-language model can do and what a human can do on the same map-reading task. Humans are trained by years of looking at maps in school, work, and daily life; they internalize the symbolic language automatically. Models have seen maps only in their training data, and not the full complexity of real-world cartography. The paper measures this gap by running each model on the same questions and comparing the accuracy.

How big is the gap? The strongest models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5-Think) achieve about 38% accuracy. Humans achieve 85%. That is a 47-percentage-point gap. This gap is the hidden quantity the benchmark reveals. It exists because the benchmark includes the full texture of real maps: multiple symbolic layers, orientation cues, scale calculations, and cross-map reasoning. Simpler benchmarks hide this gap because they test only one layer at a time.

heat.caption: Darker areas are harder for models. Multi-map retrieval and fusion, symbol decoding, and orientation are where models stumble.

reads.html: The gap is the difference in accuracy: humans at 84.87%, best models at 38.20%. That is a 46-point gap.

Table 1 and Figure 3 stratify the gap by spatial relation type (topological, metric, directional) and setting (direct vs. contextual). The error analysis assigns each failure to a category: symbol confusion, scale misinterpretation, orientation error, or multi-map coordination.

mechanism.h2: Why the benchmark exposes the gap
paras: A benchmark is only as good as the questions it asks. If you ask simple questions, even weak models will pass and you learn nothing. If you ask questions that require deep understanding, weak models fail and you see where they are stuck.

FRIEDA asks hard questions because it sources real maps—not synthetic ones, not simplified ones. Real maps have layers: a river shown with a blue line, a road with a red line, a town boundary with a dotted line, all labeled with tiny text. A legend explains what each symbol means. A compass arrow points north. A number says 5 miles per inch. A person reading the map integrates all of this. They translate symbols into concepts (What does the blue line represent?), they use spatial reasoning (If this point is north of that line, and this region is to the east of the compass line, then ...), and when the question spans two maps, they retrieve the right maps and fuse the information.

The benchmark tests this by requiring multi-step reasoning—where you have to think through several connected ideas before you can answer. A simple question is "Is city A north of city B?" A hard question is "Using the elevation map and the geological map, which rock formation is in the valley to the north of the town?" That question forces the model to understand symbols, read text, calculate bearings, retrieve both maps, and combine their information.

stages.s: Real map image(s), question text, legends and scales
Decode symbols: what do colors, lines, hatching mean?
Read text labels and extract numbers (distances, elevations, coordinates)
Reason spatially: apply topological, metric, or directional logic
Multi-map fusion (if needed): retrieve the other map and integrate its information
Answer: a spatial fact (yes/no, a location, a distance, a direction)

math.h2: How to measure the reasoning gap
math.equation: gap = A_human - A_model, where A is the fraction of correct answers
symbols: fraction of questions a human answers correctly
fraction of questions the vision-language model answers correctly
the cartographic reasoning gap we want to measure and close

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a benchmark has 100 map questions.
The best model answers 38 correctly. So A_model = 38/100 = 0.38 = 38%.
This means models are 47 points behind on map reasoning—a massive gap compared to other tasks (where gaps are often 5–10 points).

math.note: The larger the gap, the more progress is needed. FRIEDA shows a 47-point gap, proving that cartographic reasoning is a frontier for vision-language models.

items.html: The model assigns the wrong meaning to a symbol. For example, confusing a hatched region for "unstable ground" with a hatched region for "urban area" because it only sees the pattern, not the legend.
The model ignores or misinterprets the scale bar. It guesses a distance without checking the scale-to-mile ratio, leading to off-by-factor-of-ten errors.
The model does not properly use the compass arrow or north indicator. It answers "north" when the feature is actually "south" or confuses relative directions.
In the contextual setting (where the model must find the right maps first), it retrieves the wrong map or misses a map it needs, then reasons correctly on incomplete information.
A model that decodes the full symbolic layer, integrates spatial cues, accurately measures using the scale, and for multi-map questions, finds and fuses the relevant maps.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple map-reading system that a person can test interactively. Load one real map, present a question that requires decoding a symbol plus calculating a distance plus using an orientation cue (multi-step), and ask the model to answer. Show the human the model's reasoning (which symbols it identified, what scale it used, what direction it inferred) so the errors are visible. Then repeat with a cross-map question: provide two related maps and a question that requires information from both, and show how the model does at retrieving the right map and fusing the data.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = number_correct / total_questions, broken_by: (topological, metric, directional) x (single_map, multi_map_direct, multi_map_retrieval)
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that the model struggles hardest on multi-step spatial reasoning and cross-map retrieval, and that mistakes are not random—they follow patterns of symbol confusion, scale misreading, or orientation error.
